{{Short description|American mathematician (1947–2019)}}
'''Roger Charles Alperin''' (January 8, 1947 – November 21, 2019) was an American mathematician, best known for his work in [[group theory]], including its connections with [[geometry]] and [[topology]].  He was a professor at the [[University of Oklahoma]] and at [[San Jose State University]].

==Education and career==
Alperin was born on January 8, 1947, in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]].<ref name="ijg">{{cite journal|title=In Memoriam: Roger Charles Alperin (1947 - 2019)|journal=International Journal of Geometry|date=2020|volume=9|issue=1|pages=42–43|url=https://ijgeometry.com/wp-content/uploads/2020/03/4.-42-43.pdf|accessdate=December 22, 2020}}</ref>  He received a bachelor's degree from the [[University of Chicago]],<ref>{{cite book|title= American Men & Women of Science|edition=22nd|isbn= 0787674001|publisher= Thomson Gale|date=2005}}</ref> and his PhD from [[Rice University]] in 1973.  His thesis was supervised by [[Stephen M. Gersten]], and was titled ''Whitehead Torsion of Finite Abelian Groups''.<ref>{{MathGenealogy| 29565}}</ref>  After temporary positions at [[Brown University]], [[Haverford College]], and [[Washington University in St. Louis]], Alperin took a permanent position at the [[University of Oklahoma]] in 1978.<ref name="notices">{{cite journal|title=Roger Alperin|last1=Farb|first1=Benson|last2=Shalev|first2=Peter|journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society|publisher=American Mathematical Society|volume=67|issue=11|date=December 2020|doi=10.1090/noti2189|pages=1768–1769|doi-access=free}}</ref>  He was eventually promoted to full professor at the University of Oklahoma, but resigned his position to move to California in 1987.<ref name="notices"/>  Upon moving to California, he found a position at San Jose State University, which he held until his retirement in 2015.<ref name="notices"/>

Alperin died on November 21, 2019, at his home in [[Carlsbad, California]].<ref name="notices"/>

==Research==
Alperin's work on [[real tree|real trees]] in the 80s (partly joint with [[Hyman Bass]] and Kenneth Moss) helped to stimulate interest in these objects, and helped establish them as a basic tool in [[geometric group theory]].<ref name="notices"/>  Alperin has also done foundational work on the [[Mathematics and art|mathematical theory]] of [[origami]].<ref name="ijg"/>
